prompt: What is the most useful way to think of a model used as a judge?
hint: The lesson names the common mistake first.

choices.text: A neutral reader outside the system
choices.why: That is the mistake the lesson names.

choices.text: A prompt with an error rate
choices.why: Right, and habits: one more part of the system to measure.

choices.text: A replacement for the test set
choices.why: It has to be measured against one.

choices.text: A deterministic grader, like the `json` check
choices.why: Its verdict depends on order and length, as the lesson measures.

prompt: Why does `prompts/judge.txt` ask which of two replies is better rather than for a mark out of ten?
hint: What does a mark need that a comparison does not?

choices.text: Marks cost more tokens on every call to the judge
choices.why: The cost difference is negligible.

choices.text: A comparison removes position bias
choices.why: A comparison is exactly where position bias appears.

choices.text: Models cannot count to ten
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so.

choices.text: A mark needs an agreed meaning for each number
choices.why: Right: *which of these two* is one question.

prompt: In the stand-in's judge, being shown first is worth 0.6 and each character 0.006. How many characters longer must a reply be to gain as much as the first seat?
hint: Divide.

prompt: The stand-in's two biases are declared constants. How would you find biases like them in a real judge?
hint: You cannot read a real model's source.

choices.text: By measuring its verdicts against a person's
choices.why: Right, and by changing one thing at a time, such as the order.

choices.text: By asking the judge whether it is biased
choices.why: Its answer is one more reply to measure.

choices.text: By reading the provider's documentation for the bias constants
choices.why: A real model has no such constants to read.

choices.text: By raising the temperature until the bias disappears
choices.why: That adds noise; it removes nothing.

prompt: The judge agrees with the person on 10 of 16 pairs. Why is that less impressive than 62.5% sounds?
hint: How often would a coin agree?

choices.text: Sixteen is a round number
choices.why: The size of the set is not the argument here.

choices.text: Chance alone agrees about half the time
choices.why: Right, with two possible answers. Kappa measures what is left beyond that.

choices.text: The person was wrong on six of the sixteen pairs
choices.why: The person's verdict is the reference.

choices.text: The judge was run at temperature 0, without samples
choices.why: Temperature is not why agreement flatters.

prompt: The statistic that measures how far two raters agree beyond what chance would produce is Cohen's ___.
hint: A Greek letter.

prompt: The person chose `a` in 8 of 16 pairs and the judge in 10 of 16. What agreement would chance alone produce, as a fraction?
hint: Both say a, plus both say b.

prompt: A different judge agrees with people on 80% of pairs, and chance agreement for it is 0.5. What is its kappa?
hint: (observed − chance) / (1 − chance).

prompt: What does a kappa of 0 mean?
hint: It is not the same as never agreeing.

choices.text: The judge never agrees with people
choices.why: It can agree half the time and still score 0.

choices.text: Agreement no better than chance
choices.why: Right: nothing beyond what a coin would do.

choices.text: Perfect agreement
choices.why: That is 1.

choices.text: The judge refused to answer
choices.why: Kappa is computed from the answers given.

prompt: With `--swap`, on how many of the 16 pairs did the judge change its verdict?
hint: Count the `FLIP` lines.

prompt: `j03`, `j08` and `j10` agreed with the person in the first run and flipped when swapped. What was that first agreement worth?
hint: Which reply did the judge pick each time?

choices.text: It was the judge's best work on the whole set
choices.why: It picked the first reply both times.

choices.text: Nothing: an accident of seating
choices.why: Right: the person happened to prefer the reply the judge read first.

choices.text: It proves the person was biased too
choices.why: The person's verdict does not depend on the order shown to the judge.

choices.text: It counts double when kappa is computed
choices.why: Kappa counts each pair once.

prompt: Why does swapping the order not catch the judge's mistake in `j16`?
hint: What stays the same when the order changes?

choices.text: The longer reply is longer in both orders
choices.why: Right: verbosity bias survives the swap.

choices.text: `j16` was left out when the pairs were swapped
choices.why: Every pair is asked twice.

choices.text: The person's verdict for `j16` is the wrong one
choices.why: `a` answers the question; `b` says nothing.

choices.text: Position bias only affects short replies
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so.

prompt: Which paper does the lesson cite for position and verbosity bias in LLM judges?
hint: Named after a benchmark and an arena.

choices.text: *Language Models are Few-Shot Learners* (Brown and others, 2020)
choices.why: That one is lesson 1's, about examples.

choices.text: *Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations* (Min and others, 2022)
choices.why: Also lesson 1's, about what examples teach.

choices.text: *Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena* (Zheng and others, 2023)
choices.why: Right. It also found strong judges agreed with people about as often as people agreed with each other.

choices.text: Cohen's 1960 paper on agreement
choices.why: That one gave us kappa.

prompt: Which of these reduce the damage a judge's biases do? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four mitigations were given.

choices.text: Ask in both orders and drop verdicts that flip
choices.why: Yes: ten stable verdicts, seven right.

choices.text: Calibrate against people and report kappa
choices.why: Yes, on the task the judge will do.

choices.text: Keep a person reading a sample of verdicts
choices.why: Yes, for as long as the judge is in use.

choices.text: Show the longer reply second
choices.why: That trades one bias against the other and measures neither.

prompt: Why does this platform grade every question with a deterministic grader rather than a model judge?
hint: Who checks a verdict after it is given?

choices.text: Model judges are too expensive to run on every single answer students give
choices.why: Cost is not the reason given.

choices.text: No person checks the verdict, so it has to be the same every time
choices.why: Right: there is no human reviewer between the key and the student.

choices.text: Judges cannot read Portuguese
choices.why: Language has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: Deterministic graders are more accurate on essays
choices.why: They cannot grade essays at all, which is why essays are excluded.

prompt: The platform's algebra grader samples at fixed points, never random ones. What failure is that rule guarding against?
hint: Tuesday and Thursday.

choices.text: Slow grading when many students sit an exam
choices.why: Speed is not the concern.

choices.text: Students working out the sample points in advance
choices.why: The rule is about consistency, not secrecy.

choices.text: Expressions that differ at a single point
choices.why: That is a known limit of sampling, not what this rule is for.

choices.text: One answer, two verdicts on two days
choices.why: Right: marked right one day and wrong the next. A judge with position bias does exactly that.

prompt: A team wants to grade free-text answers in a certification exam with a judge whose kappa against teachers is 0.85. Using this lesson, what is still the objection?
hint: Where is the verdict checked?

choices.text: A kappa of 0.85 is too low to mean anything
choices.why: It is high agreement; that is not the objection.

choices.text: Kappa only works with two answers
choices.why: Cohen's kappa works with any number of categories.

choices.text: In an exam the verdict is final, with nobody to catch the remaining errors
choices.why: Right: a judge belongs where something else catches its mistakes.

choices.text: Judges cannot read long answers
choices.why: They read them; they tend to prefer them.

prompt: Match each use of a judge to what catches its mistakes.
hint: In each, something else checks.

pairs.right: The person who edits the top one

pairs.left: Choosing which replies a person reads first
pairs.right: The person, who still reads them

pairs.left: Tracking the share of poor replies week by week
pairs.right: A steady bias moving both weeks alike

prompt: Put the steps of bringing a judge into use in order.
hint: Labels come before the judge is consulted.
items: People label a sample of the real task without seeing the judge
Run the judge on the sample in both orders
Compute kappa on the verdicts that do not flip
Use it where something else checks it, with a person reading a sample

prompt: A judge picks the longer reply in 14 of 16 pairs, and people pick it in 7. Its raw agreement with people is 9 of 16. What do you conclude?
hint: Compare the two rates of choosing the longer reply.

choices.text: Its verdicts follow length; it is not ready
choices.why: Right: 14 against 7 is the bias, and 9 of 16 is near a coin.

choices.text: It is fine: 9 of 16 is a majority
choices.why: A coin would get about 8.

choices.text: People are biased towards short replies
choices.why: People are the reference here.

choices.text: Swap the order of the replies and it will be fixed
choices.why: A swap cannot catch a length preference.
